name: Patmos
summary: Aegean island where the seer John says he was when he received the Revelation.
historicalContext: Patmos lay off the western coast of Roman Asia in the Aegean. Revelation 1:9 is the primary evidence for John’s presence there.
archaeology: The island is certain; no first-century archaeological feature identifies the exact place where the visions were experienced.

confidence.explanation: The island named in Revelation is securely identified with modern Patmos. The exact location on the island is unknown.

name: Cave of the Apocalypse — traditional site
summary: Later Christian tradition identifies this cave on Patmos with John’s visionary experience.
historicalContext: The tradition is important for reception history but is not first-century archaeological evidence.

confidence.explanation: The cave is a major later Christian traditional site; Revelation itself does not identify a cave and archaeology cannot verify it as John’s location.

name: Smyrna
summary: Major port city of Roman Asia and the second of Revelation’s seven churches.
historicalContext: Smyrna was a prosperous Roman provincial city with strong imperial associations. Much visible archaeology belongs to later rebuilding, especially after the 178 CE earthquake.

confidence.explanation: Ancient Smyrna is securely identified beneath and around modern Izmir.

name: Pergamum
summary: Former Attalid capital and third church addressed in Revelation.
historicalContext: Pergamum was a major political, religious, and cultural center of Roman Asia, with prominent temples and imperial-cult institutions.

confidence.explanation: The ancient city is securely identified at Bergama/Pergamon.

name: Great Altar of Pergamum
summary: Monumental Hellenistic altar from Pergamum, sometimes proposed as background to the phrase “Satan’s throne.”
historicalContext: The altar predates Revelation and was a prominent part of Pergamum’s monumental landscape.
archaeology: Its identification as the specific referent of Revelation 2:13 is speculative; imperial cult, the acropolis, and other interpretations also exist.

confidence.explanation: The altar itself is established archaeology; connecting it specifically to “Satan’s throne” is only one modern interpretation.

interpretations.title: Great Altar as “Satan’s throne” background
interpretations.summary: A visually striking proposal, but Revelation does not name the altar and no consensus establishes this identification.

name: Thyatira
summary: Commercial city of Lydia and fourth church addressed in Revelation.
historicalContext: Ancient Thyatira occupied the site of modern Akhisar. Epigraphic evidence from the city is important for its associations and occupational groups.

confidence.explanation: The ancient city is securely located at modern Akhisar, though much lies beneath the modern city.

name: Sardis
summary: Ancient Lydian capital and fifth church addressed in Revelation.
historicalContext: Sardis retained major urban importance in Roman Asia. Its acropolis and lower-city archaeology illuminate the setting but do not mechanically explain Revelation’s metaphors.

confidence.explanation: Sardis is securely identified at the archaeological site near modern Sart.

name: Philadelphia of Lydia
summary: Sixth church addressed in Revelation, located in the Lydian interior of Roman Asia.
historicalContext: The ancient city lies under modern Alaşehir; earthquakes and continuous occupation complicate archaeological reconstruction.

confidence.explanation: Ancient Philadelphia is securely identified with modern Alaşehir, though first-century remains are limited.

name: Roman province of Asia — Revelation setting
summary: Broad provincial setting of the seven churches.
historicalContext: “Asia” in Revelation 1:4 means the Roman province, not the modern continent. The map anchor represents a broad administrative landscape, not a capital point or exact border.

confidence.explanation: The province is historically established; this point is only a display anchor and its boundaries varied over time.

name: Babylon the Great — visionary city
summary: Revelation’s symbolic “Babylon” is a visionary city and political-religious image, not plotted as the archaeological city of Babylon.
historicalContext: Many interpreters see Rome as the primary first-century referent, while the imagery deliberately draws on biblical Babylon and broader imperial critique.

confidence.explanation: The text presents symbolic geography. Historical Babylon and Rome remain separate real-world places; this visionary entity receives no terrestrial coordinate.

interpretations.title: Rome as primary first-century referent
interpretations.summary: The seven hills/kings, imperial power, commerce, and persecution imagery make Rome a strong first-century referent, without exhausting the symbol.

interpretations.title: Historical Babylon in Mesopotamia
interpretations.summary: The ancient city supplies deep biblical imagery, but most modern historical readings do not treat Revelation 17–18 as a simple geographic prediction about the Mesopotamian ruins.

name: Har-Magedon / Armageddon — visionary toponym
summary: Revelation 16:16 names Har-Magedon in an apocalyptic battle scene. Its etymology and relationship to historical Megiddo are debated.

confidence.explanation: The text gives a name but no recoverable battle coordinate. Linking it directly to Tell Megiddo is an interpretation, not an established site identification.

interpretations.title: Association with Megiddo
interpretations.summary: The name is commonly connected with Megiddo, a strategic biblical site, but the linguistic form and lack of a literal “Mount Megiddo” make the equation less simple than popular maps suggest.

name: Heavenly throne room — visionary space
summary: Revelation 4–5 describes a heavenly throne room with worship, living creatures, elders, and the Lamb.

confidence.explanation: This is visionary/theological space and is not assigned terrestrial coordinates.

name: The Abyss — visionary space
summary: Apocalyptic realm appearing in Revelation’s trumpet and beast imagery.

confidence.explanation: The Abyss is visionary cosmological imagery, not an archaeological place.

name: Gog and Magog — visionary nations
summary: Revelation 20 reuses Ezekiel’s Gog/Magog imagery for nations gathered from the earth after the millennium.

confidence.explanation: The passage explicitly universalizes the imagery to nations at the earth’s corners; it should not be mapped onto a modern country.
Visionary eschatological imagery; no terrestrial coordinate is appropriate.

name: New Jerusalem — visionary city
aliases: Jerusalem coming down out of heaven
summary: Revelation 21–22 portrays a New Jerusalem descending from heaven, with immense symbolic dimensions, gates, foundations, river, and tree of life.
historicalContext: The city reworks Jerusalem, temple, Eden, prophetic restoration, and cosmic imagery. It is deliberately visualized outside ordinary map mode.

confidence.explanation: The text explicitly presents a visionary city descending from heaven. Plotting it as a modern archaeological coordinate would misrepresent the genre.

name: River and tree of life — visionary landscape
aliases: River of the water of life
summary: Revelation 22 reunites river, city, throne, and tree-of-life imagery in the final vision.

confidence.explanation: Visionary imagery consciously echoing Eden and prophetic temple-river traditions; no terrestrial watercourse is claimed.
